column1: Standard epicardial wire configuration after cardiac surgery, and where do the wires emerge?
column2: Two wires on the RA and two on the RV. RA wires emerge through skin to the RIGHT of the sternum; RV wires to the LEFT. Each wire is lightly sutured to myocardium at one end.

column1: Haemodynamic benefit of preserving atrial contraction (atrial / AV-sequential pacing vs ventricular-only)?
column2: Atrial contraction augments ventricular preloading and can raise cardiac output by up to ~25%. Matters most in reduced ventricular compliance (ischaemia, hypertrophy), where loss of atrial kick markedly drops CO.

column1: Southampton wire colour convention and does polarity within a pair matter?
column2: Blue = ventricle, white = atrium. Which wire of a pair goes to the +ve or -ve port is of no consequence (same for both chambers). But you MUST confirm A and V leads are in the correct ports.

column1: Default mode and rate when the external box is switched on, and typical mode/rate leaving theatre?
column2: Default: DDD at 60 with preset sensing/output for a standard patient. Most patients leave theatre DDD at 80–90 to optimise CO. Chronic AF may be VVI or DVI instead.

column1: Define sensitivity in temporary pacing.
column2: The minimum intrinsic signal amplitude (mV) the pacemaker will register as a sensed event. It is the input/detection side of the box (contrast with output/capture).

column1: Relationship between the sensitivity NUMBER and how sensitive the box is?
column2: Inverse. A LOWER number = MORE sensitive (detects smaller signals). Think of the number as fence height: lower fence, more beats get seen. So 1 mV is more sensitive than 5 mV.

column1: How do you measure the sensing threshold at the bedside?
column2: Demand mode (AAI/VVI/DDD), rate set BELOW intrinsic. Increase the number (less sensitive) until the sense indicator stops flashing and the box paces asynchronously — don't sustain (R-on-T risk). Then decrease the number until the indicator flashes with each P/R wave; the first value at which sensing returns is the sensing threshold.

column1: Where should sensitivity be set relative to the measured threshold, and why?
column2: At roughly HALF the sensing threshold. This gives margin to detect abnormally small signals and to compensate for peri-lead fibrosis reducing the signal over time. E.g. threshold 4 mV → set ~2 mV.

column1: What sensitivity is set when there is NO intrinsic rhythm?
column2: The threshold can't be measured, so sensitivity is set empirically to ~2 mV.

column1: OVERSENSING — cause direction, consequence, and fix?
column2: Cause: number too LOW / too sensitive. Box sees T waves, R waves, myopotentials or diathermy and treats them as intrinsic beats → INAPPROPRIATE INHIBITION → pauses/asystole (dangerous if pacing-dependent). Fix: RAISE the number (make it less sensitive); remove the interfering source.

column1: UNDERSENSING — cause direction, consequence, and fix?
column2: Cause: number too HIGH / not sensitive enough. Intrinsic beats missed → box paces regardless → competing/asynchronous spikes → R-on-T risk. Fix: LOWER the number (more sensitive); if it persists the electrogram is too small → check lead contact, switch to the other wire pair.

column1: Why are asynchronous (OO) modes chosen when diathermy is in use?
column2: In demand modes, diathermy can be OVERSENSED and inhibit output — dangerous with no underlying rhythm. AOO/VOO/DOO have no sensing at all, so they pace regardless of interference.

column1: Which pacing modes have NO sensing function?
column2: The 'OO' asynchronous modes: AOO, VOO, DOO. The third NBG letter O = no response to sensing.

column1: Define the capture (stimulation) threshold.
column2: The minimum pacemaker OUTPUT required to reliably depolarise the myocardium (produce an action potential). This is the output side — distinct from the sensing threshold.

column1: Method to measure the ventricular capture threshold?
column2: Set VVI, rate ~10 bpm above the patient's rate, output 2.5 V. Slowly decrease output until capture is lost, then increase until capture returns — that value is the capture threshold.

column1: Safe output setting once the capture threshold is known?
column2: 5.0 V OR 3× the threshold, whichever is GREATER. Keep output ≥5 V unless special circumstances dictate otherwise.

column1: Electrical capture vs mechanical capture — why does it matter?
column2: An electrical spike/depolarisation on ECG does NOT guarantee myocardial contraction. Always confirm mechanical capture with a mechanical signal — arterial pressure trace or pulse oximeter waveform — not the ECG alone.

column1: Time course of capture-threshold rise, and figures for wire failure?
column2: Thresholds rise from inflammation at the wire–myocardium interface, accelerated by higher energy. Notable rise commonly after ~4 days; failure to pace in >60% of right and >80% of left atrial wires by day 5 — hence day 4–5 is when permanent pacing is considered.

column1: Why must you NOT check the capture threshold if there is no underlying rhythm?
column2: Losing capture during the test may be impossible to reverse (no fallback rhythm). Instead, watch for occasional MISSED BEATS as the warning sign of a rising threshold.

column1: What do the first three positions of the NBG code denote?
column2: Position 1 = chamber PACED, Position 2 = chamber SENSED, Position 3 = RESPONSE to sensing (I inhibited, T triggered, D dual, O none). Only these first 3 are relevant to temporary epicardial pacing (O/A/V/D).

column1: Describe DDD behaviour.
column2: Waits for intrinsic atrial event; if none, paces the atrium. Then waits for intrinsic ventricular event (after the atrial event, paced or sensed); if none, paces the ventricle. Ventricular pacing can TRACK atrial activity above the lower rate limit.

column1: Why is DDD problematic in rapid atrial arrhythmia, and what is preferred?
column2: DDD tracks the fast atrial rate and paces the ventricle too rapidly. DDI (or mode-switch) is preferred as it does not track the atrium.

column1: AAI — indication and contraindications?
column2: Indication: relative bradycardia with intact, reliable AV conduction and an atrial rhythm too slow to compete. Contraindicated in AF/flutter and atrial tachycardia (can't capture atrium) and in AV node block.

column1: VVI — indication and key limitation?
column2: Indication: when atrial pacing is futile, e.g. AF. Same as AAI but sensing/pacing in the ventricle. Limitation: no atrial contribution to ventricular preload (loss of atrial kick).

column1: DOO — its two notable specific indications?
column2: (1) AV-sequential pacing when a synchronous mode is contraindicated (e.g. diathermy) in a patient who benefits from atrial kick. (2) Emergency management of pacemaker-mediated tachycardia.

column1: The three categories of temporary pacing failure?
column2: 1) Failure to CAPTURE (spike present, no myocardial response). 2) Failure to SENSE (under- or over-sensing). 3) Failure to OUTPUT (no spike at all).

column1: Stepwise approach to FAILURE TO CAPTURE?
column2: 1) Confirm — put monitor in pacemaker/spike-enhanced mode. 2) Increase output to max. 3) Reversible causes: hyperkalaemia, acidosis, hypoxia, antiarrhythmics, hypothermia. 4) Circuit: connections, wire integrity, battery; try reversing polarity or the other wire pair. 5) No rhythm = emergency → transcutaneous pacing + defibrillator ready.

column1: First monitor-related step when a pacing spike appears absent on a digital ECG?
column2: Select the pacemaker/spike-enhanced monitor mode. Digital high-frequency filters strip the brief pacing spike, so 'no spike' may be an artefact of filtering rather than true failure to output.

column1: Managing UNDERSENSING?
column2: Increase sensitivity (LOWER the number). If it persists, the intrinsic electrogram is too small → check lead contact/position and switch to the alternate wires. Beware competing spikes / R-on-T while unresolved.

column1: Managing OVERSENSING?
column2: Decrease sensitivity (RAISE the number). Identify the source — T waves, diathermy, myopotentials, external interference. If the patient is pacing-dependent or diathermy is in use, switch to an asynchronous mode (VOO/DOO).

column1: Causes of FAILURE TO OUTPUT (no spike at all)?
column2: Box off or locked; flat battery; loose or fractured wire/connection; or oversensing masquerading as no-output (box thinks it sees intrinsic activity and inhibits).

column1: 'Box appears dead' — quickest checks?
column2: Is it ON and UNLOCKED? These boxes must be ON to program and are then LOCKED with the yellow key button — a seemingly dead box may just be off or locked. Then check battery and connections.

column1: Microshock risk with epicardial wires and the precautions?
column2: Wires are low-resistance connections directly to the heart → microshock can precipitate arrhythmia, especially VF. Handle only with non-conductive gloves; discharge static on a large metal object (e.g. the bed) first; insulate wires in a non-conductive container when unused; nurse in a cardiac-protected environment.

column1: Minimum monitoring for any patient with temporary pacing?
column2: Continuous ECG monitoring PLUS immediate access to a cardiac defibrillator with transcutaneous pacing capability (because of failure/arrhythmia risk).

column1: Rationale for 'back-up' pacing at a rate of 40?
column2: Lets the patient stay in their intrinsic rhythm until significant haemodynamic compromise, while allowing the sensing threshold to be continuously monitored — so full pacing can be resumed with confidence the threshold hasn't become excessive.

column1: Epicardial wire removal — timing, technique, and what to observe for?
column2: Usually ~day 4 on the surgeon's instruction (by CICU nurses). Constant gentle traction; if caught by a tight suture, pull as far as safe then cut close to skin (ends retract — no adverse effect). Observe a few hours for: tamponade, ventricular arrhythmia, damage to coronary anastomoses.

column1: Heparin protocol around wire removal?
column2: Stop heparin, remove wires after 2 hours (no APTR check needed). Remove the Redivac drain 1 hour later if no pericardial bleeding, then restart heparin immediately. Checking an APTR only delays removal — high-risk in mechanical-valve patients.

column1: IABP + pacing interaction and how to avoid it?
column2: If the IABP triggers off the ECG, pacing spikes can be misread as QRS complexes. Keep the high-frequency filter ON, or time the IABP off the arterial waveform instead.

column1: Risk factors for needing a PERMANENT pacemaker after cardiac surgery?
column2: Older age, pre-operative bundle branch block, prolonged CPB, and suboptimal intra-operative myocardial protection. Common indications: CHB, sinus node dysfunction, slow ventricular response in AF, Mobitz II with inadequate rate.

column1: Terminology pitfall: what exactly is the value found when the sense indicator first flashes again?
column2: It is the SENSING threshold (the smallest signal reliably sensed) — NOT the capture/stimulation threshold. Keep the two distinct: sensing = input side, capture = output side. (The Southampton page loosely calls it the 'pacing threshold'.)
